title: Latching and seal-in
summary: Give the motor a memory: the output holds itself on after Start is released until Stop is pressed.

sections.heading: The output remembers
sections.body: Include the output itself as an alternative to Start: once running, the motor keeps its own condition TRUE. This is the **seal-in** or self-holding circuit.

sections.heading: The seal-in rung
sections.body: In relay logic the auxiliary contact bridges the Start button.

sections.heading: Seal-in in ST
sections.body: Stop and the overload relay come after the OR, so they always win.
sections.code: MotorContactor := (StartPB OR MotorContactor) AND StopPB AND OverloadOK;

sections.heading: Common mistake
sections.body: `StartPB OR (MotorContactor AND StopPB)` gives Start priority: holding Start keeps the motor running even while Stop is pressed.

question.question: With the correct seal-in, what happens if Start and Stop are pressed together?
question.explanation: StopPB is FALSE and AND-ed after the OR, so the result is FALSE.

sections.heading: Practice: motor start/stop
sections.body: Build the seal-in for the conveyor and let the checker test start, stop priority and the overload trip.

sections.heading: Summary and troubleshooting note
sections.body:
A seal-in latch uses the output as its own condition; stop conditions are AND-ed after the OR.

**Troubleshooting note:** If a motor will not stay on after Start is released, the seal-in path is missing or broken; if it cannot be stopped, check stop priority.

checkpoint.question: What keeps a latched motor running after Start is released?
options: The output itself in its own condition
